meaning: Each tie names the phrase of the paper that a Lean declaration states, as read side by side for Proof Reader (wcook04/proof-reader 79fe18157a1d, papers/pcp-reading-guide). Titles, reading notes, topics and comparisons are AI-drafted or AI-assessed; no mathematician has reviewed them.

topics.name: PCP theorem
topics.description: Polynomial-time verification with logarithmic randomness and a constant number of proof-bit queries characterizes NP.

topics.name: Polynomial distance
topics.description: The Schwartz–Zippel bound limits the fraction of points where a nonzero polynomial vanishes.

topics.name: Low-degree extension
topics.description: Interpolation represents a table on a grid by a unique polynomial with a degree bound in each variable.

topics.name: Labels and encoding
topics.description: Polynomial labels turn field values and their polynomial expressions into bits and distinguish full, affine and homogeneous observations.

topics.name: Verifier and query trees
topics.description: A verifier selects an adaptive query tree from its input and random seed, with explicit acceptance probabilities and proof-address bounds.

topics.name: Polynomial-time implementation
topics.description: A finite multi-stack machine implements the verifier or witness checker with polynomial running time.

topics.name: Colouring constraints
topics.description: Vertex values and edge differences satisfy polynomial equations exactly when they define a proper three-colouring.

topics.name: Vanishing certificates
topics.description: A polynomial vanishing on a grid admits a decomposition using the coordinate vanishing polynomials and a certificate expressed by two identities.

topics.name: Linearity and self-correction
topics.description: Linearity testing finds a nearby linear word, and two randomly shifted queries recover a requested value with controlled error.

topics.name: Queries, randomness and repetition
topics.description: Query counts, fair-bit sampling, proof length and independent repetition give the resource bounds and final soundness error.

topics.name: Proof tables and checks
topics.description: Four pairs of points and lines tables supply the answers read by four low-degree tests, two grid tests and a difference check.

topics.name: Binary low-degree test
topics.description: Small rejection gives one polynomial whose encoding is close to the points table on both full and homogeneous labels.

topics.name: Zero-on-grid test
topics.description: Corrected certificate queries test vanishing identities at prescribed points and relate failure on the grid to rejection.

topics.name: Completeness and soundness
topics.description: An honest colouring passes every check, while sufficiently small rejection forces four nearby polynomials to describe a proper colouring.

topics.name: Reduction to three-colouring
topics.description: Accepting computations become finite constraints, Boolean clauses and graphs while preserving the existence of a witness.

topics.name: NP witness verification
topics.description: A language belongs to NP when membership is witnessed by a polynomial-length string accepted by a polynomial-time checker.

topics.name: Standard low-degree test
topics.description: Weighted interpolation at generator powers tests low degree, with plurality correction turning small rejection into polynomial agreement.

topics.name: Local correction over fields
topics.description: Random line queries recover a polynomial value at a prescribed point or bound the probability of accepting a wrong value.

topics.name: Bivariate agreement
topics.description: Agreement between low-degree row and column polynomials produces a nearby bivariate polynomial and consistent values at selected crossings.

topics.name: Point-versus-line test
topics.description: Agreement with supplied line polynomials at random points yields one nearby polynomial of bounded total degree.

topics.name: Set-multilinear encoding
topics.description: Writing exponents in a fixed number of base digits replaces a line polynomial by a polynomial of fixed total degree.

topics.name: Hadamard test
topics.description: Linearity, unit, product and affine consistency checks test whether a word is close to the encoding of one field value.

topics.name: Inner low-degree test
topics.description: A random choice between Hadamard testing and a binary weighted identity tests one encoded line entry for low degree.

topics.name: Local correction on bits
topics.description: Weighted bit queries and tests of encoded line entries recover a homogeneous observation at a prescribed point, allowing rejection.

notes.PCP.InNP: The formal definition says that a certificate with the preceding properties exists. Its content depends on the chosen condition on checkers: membership means that polynomially bounded witnesses characterize the language and that their checker satisfies that condition. In the main theorem the condition requires an actual finite multi-stack Turing machine with a polynomial running-time bound.
notes.PCP.Language: A language is a set of finite binary strings. The formal definition describes it by the condition $x\in L$, rather than by an algorithm for testing that condition. It therefore includes undecidable languages. Membership in NP is a further property, supplied by a bounded-witness characterization and a polynomial-time checker.
notes.PCP.Machine.PolyTimeAlg: The formal definition requires a finite multi-stack Turing machine that computes one verifier step in polynomial time in the length of the encoded input, random string and answer history. A step outputs either a decision bit or a binary query address. This property alone does not connect the function to a particular verifier; the main theorem also requires equality with its bounded decision trees.
notes.PCP.Machine.PolyTimeRel: The formal definition requires a finite multi-stack Turing machine that computes the Boolean relation on input pairs $(x,w)$ within a fixed polynomial bound in $|x|+|w|+1$. The pair is written with one separator and the answer is a single bit. This concrete condition is the checker requirement chosen in the main theorem's definition of NP.
notes.PCP.Machine.encodePair: The pair $(x,w)$ is encoded by the symbols for $x$, followed by one separator and then the symbols for $w$. Its length is $|x|+|w|+1$, including the separator even when one string is empty. This is the input representation used when polynomial time is required for the witness-checking relation.
notes.PCP.NPCertificate: A certificate that a language belongs to NP specifies a polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients and a Boolean checker for pairs $(x,w)$. The checker must satisfy the chosen time condition, and for every input $x$ one has $x\in L$ exactly when some witness $w$ of length at most $p(|x|)$ is accepted. The time condition is still a parameter in this definition; the main theorem chooses the concrete machine model.
notes.PCP.ProofOracle: The proof is an arbitrary infinite sequence of bits $\pi(0),\pi(1),\ldots$. There is no assumption that this sequence can be computed. Finiteness of the relevant proof is expressed elsewhere: if all queried addresses are below $N$, only the first $N$ bits can affect acceptance. Completeness chooses such an oracle, while soundness quantifies over every oracle.
notes.PCP.QueryTree: A tree with bound $d$ makes at most $d$ adaptive bit queries on any path. A leaf already contains an accept-or-reject decision, and may appear before the bound is exhausted. An internal node names a proof address and has separate continuations for answers $0$ and $1$. The bound counts queries along one run, rather than the number of addresses appearing across the entire tree.
notes.PCP.QueryTree.addresses: The address set contains the address at every query node in the tree, on both branches at each split. It can contain more addresses than a single run reads, because different answer histories follow different branches. A proof-length bound is imposed by requiring every element of this set to lie below $N$, for every random string. Collecting the set alone does not impose that bound.
notes.PCP.QueryTree.eval: To evaluate a tree against a proof $\pi$, read the bit at the root query address and take the corresponding branch. Repeat until reaching a leaf, whose Boolean value is the decision. The input tree already has a finite depth bound, so evaluation follows at most that many queries. Adaptivity means later addresses may depend on earlier proof bits.
notes.PCP.Verifier: A verifier specifies a natural-number random-bit budget for each input length, one fixed natural-number query bound, and a bounded adaptive decision tree for each input and random string. These data describe which bits are read and how acceptance is decided. They do not include an efficiency assertion or a computability requirement on the budget. The main theorem adds a prescribed budget, algorithm correspondence and polynomial running time.
notes.PCP.Verifier.CanonicalRandomness: The budget must equal $a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+b$ at every input length $n$, for fixed natural-number constants $a$ and $b$. This equality determines the entire budget. A mere upper bound would leave an arbitrary length-dependent choice: a budget of either zero or one bit could encode any predicate of $n$. The prescribed formula removes that freedom; polynomial running time is still a separate requirement.
notes.PCP.Verifier.CompleteAt: At a fixed input $x$, perfect completeness means that there exists a single proof $\pi$ whose acceptance probability is $1$. The proof is chosen before the random string. Since the probability is uniform on a finite random space, this is equivalent to acceptance for every random string. The main theorem supplies this property for every input in the language.
notes.PCP.Verifier.ImplementedBy: For every input and random string, the formal definition equates the verifier's tree with the tree obtained by unfolding the algorithm from an empty answer history, using the verifier's query bound. The random index is first converted into a fixed-length binary string. The cutoff matters: after the last permitted query, another request is replaced by rejection. Thus the equality concerns bounded execution; it does not by itself prove that unrestricted execution halts within that many queries.
notes.PCP.Verifier.ReadsBelow: The formal definition bounds all addresses in every tree for input $x$, for every random string and on both answer branches. Each address must be strictly less than $N$, so the relevant positions are $0,\ldots,N-1$. The supplied congruence theorem shows that proofs agreeing on this prefix have identical acceptance probability. This expresses finite proof length while retaining infinite proof oracles.
notes.PCP.Verifier.SoundAt: At a fixed input $x$, soundness with error $s$ means that every proof $\pi$ is accepted with probability at most $s$. The universal quantifier includes arbitrary malformed or inconsistent proofs. The definition permits a rational parameter $s$; the main theorem uses $s=1/2$ on every input outside the language. The definition itself does not identify which inputs are outside the language.
notes.PCP.Verifier.accProb: For fixed $x$ and $\pi$, acceptance probability is the number of accepting random strings divided by $2^k$, where $k$ is the budget at input length $|x|$. This is an exact rational probability under independent fair random bits. The denominator is positive even when $k=0$, in which case there is one empty random string and acceptance is deterministic.
notes.PCP.Verifier.acceptingRandomness: Fix an input $x$ and a proof $\pi$. The formal definition selects the random strings for which the associated decision tree accepts when evaluated against $\pi$. If the budget is $k$ bits, these strings form a subset of the $2^k$ possible random strings. This is a set; the acceptance probability is defined separately by dividing its size by $2^k$.
notes.PCP.VerifierAlg: One step receives three finite binary strings: the input, the random bits and the answers to earlier proof queries, in their original order. It returns either a Boolean decision or a natural-number proof address to query next. The formal definition allows arbitrary such functions. Their computability and polynomial running time are imposed later, and their connection to a particular verifier requires a separate equality of bounded decision trees.
notes.PCP.np_subset_pcp: For every language $L$ in NP for the concrete machine model, the formal statement supplies one verifier and one polynomial-time step algorithm. The verifier uses at most a fixed number $q$ of proof-bit queries, exactly $a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+b$ random bits and addresses below a polynomial in $n$. Members have a proof accepted with certainty; every proof for a nonmember is accepted with probability at most $1/2$. The verifier, algorithm, constants and polynomial are fixed before the input is chosen; the proof may depend on it. Algorithm correspondence uses execution capped at the query bound.
